jñānamārga
(‘the path of ज्ञान or knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
Since very ancient times, two paths (mārga = path) have been laid out before human beings: the कर्ममार्ग and the ज्ञानमार्ग (the path of action and the path of knowledge).
In the former, a person has to perform all actions ordained by the scriptures to attain progress in worldly life and also prepare for spiritual enlightenment.
In the latter, which is supposed to be a continuation of the former and superior to it, one is expected to give up all actions save those needed for the maintenance of the body to continue sādhanās or spiritual practices.
See JÑĀNAYOGA for details.

jñānendriyas
(‘organs of knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
Acquisition of knowledge, whether temporal or spiritual, is basic to life. Though spiritual knowledge is essential for attaining लिबेरतिओन् from सṁसार or transmigratory existence, temporal know-ledge can never be ignored. It is this knowledge that helps us to live in this world. If properly utilised, it can be an asset for spiritual life too.
Since ज्ञान or sensory knowledge is acquired through the five sense-organs, viz., चक्षुस् (organ of sight), śrotra (organ of hearing), ghrāṇa (organ of smell), rasanā (organ of taste) and tvak (organ of touch), they are called ज्ञानेन्द्रियस् or organs that bring knowledge to us. In common language they are the eyes, the ears, the nose, the tongue and the skin.
They are the evolutes of the सत्त्व-part of the five primordial elements or तन्मात्रस् according to Vedānta.
These are the subtle organs located inside the physical organs like the eye, the ear etc.
See also INDRIYAS.

jñānamudrā
(‘pose of knowledge and wisdom’)
------------------------------------------
Mudrās are poses of hands which indicate or signify some idea or teaching. They are generally shown in the icons of gods and goddesses, sages and great persons.
Jñānamudrā is generally exhibited in the right hand of images of divinities like दक्षिणामूर्ति and सुब्रह्मण्य as also of ācāryas like शङ्कर and Madhva.
In this मुद्रा, the top of the fore finger is made to rest on the top of the thumb, the other three fingers being shown either straight or slightly bent. It suggests the absorption of the जीव in ब्रह्मन् or God.
Sometimes, the right hand in this pose is kept on the heart and the left hand with the palm facing upwards is placed on the left thigh. This is said to be dear to Śrī राम.
See also MUDRĀS.

jñātṛtva
(‘the capacity to know’)
------------------------------------------
All the six systems of Hindu philo-sophy accept the जीव or the jīvātman as a fundamental aspect of च्रेअतिओन् and the created world. He has three capacities: ज्ञातृत्व (the capacity to know); कर्तृत्व (the capacity to perform actions) and bhoktṛtva (the capacity to experience the results of these actions). Hence he is called jñātṛ (the knower), kartṛ (doer) and भोक्तृ (enjoyer or experiencer).
These three capacities distinguish him from प्रकृति or the insentient nature and are therefore a sign of life and चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्.
See also BHOKTṚ.

jñāna-कर्म-samuccaya-vāda
(‘The school [which accepts that] ज्ञान or knowledge and कर्म or ritualistic action can be combined’)
------------------------------------------
At one stage, in the growth of the polemical literature of Vedānta, one of the bones of contention was whether ज्ञान or knowledge of the आत्मन् and कर्म or ritualistic action could be combined. The school that advocated the possibility of the combination came to be known as ‘jñānakarmasamuccayavāda’. It was mostly the Viśiṣṭādvaita of Rāmānuja (A.
-1137) that subscribed to this view. The advaitins including शङ्कर (A.

-820) opposed it vehemently.
The doctrine needs some elaboration. According to the dualistic schools of Vedānta, ब्रह्मन् (God), the jīvas (the individual souls) and the world are all different from one another. Hence, even after a जीव, the individual सोउल् in bondage, realises his आत्मन्-nature through ज्ञान, as the pure spirit different from the body-मिन्द् complex, he continues to perceive the world and the other jīvas as existing and as different from himself. Hence he has no problem in performing कर्म or actions prescribed by the scriptures as his duties, as long as he continues to live in the body which is a product of his past (or prārabdha) karmas. So, combining कर्म or ritualistic actions and ordained duties, with his ज्ञान or subjective realisation of his being the आत्मन् or the pure spirit, is not at all a problem.
However, according to the Advaita Vedānta of शङ्कर, ब्रह्मन्, आत्मन् (the true nature of the जीव) and the world outside are all one and the same. Since the jīvas and the world are illusory perceptions—like the perception of a snake in a rope in semi-darkness—which इल्लुसिओन् will disappear on the rise of ज्ञान or direct and immediate perception of the truth as it is, a jñāni (man of knowledge, the liberated सोउल्) will not see anything outside himself or as different from himself. He will see only one reality, the one without a second. Hence it is impossible for him to do any कर्म or rituals which presupposes the perception of duality. Consequently, sarvakarma parityāga or totally giving up all actions, will come to him most naturally. So, jñānakarma-samuccaya is simply out of question.
If कृष्ण could teach the Bhagavad-gītā to अर्जुन or शङ्कर himself could do so much work in his life-time as vanquishing the opponents or writing philosophical treatises or making disciples or establishing Maṭhas one will be forced to concede that jñānakarmasamuccaya is possible. Otherwise one has to come to the unpleasant conclusion that neither of them was enlightened!
What शङ्कर perhaps meant was that desire-motivated or selfish action was not possible for a jñāni though लोकसङ्ग्रह or unselfish service to the world was always possible.

Jñānārṇava Tantra
------------------------------------------
This is an important tantra work mainly devoted to the श्रीविद्या (See ŚRĪVIDYĀ) or the Divine मोथेर् as ललिता-त्रिपुरसुन्दरी. It has 26 paṭalas or chapters containing 1711 ślokas.
A very brief summary of the contents may be given here as follows:
Paṭala 1 (28 verses)
This contains a description of the 50 letters of the Sanskrit alphabet as ‘Mātṛkās’ (‘little mothers’) and declares them as शब्द-ब्रह्मन् from which the universe evolves in course of time.
This section also refers to the famous Haṁsamantra (“so’ham haṁsaḥ”) as referring to Śabdātīta-ब्रह्मन्.
Paṭala 2 (76 verses)
This describes the famous Bālā- मन्त्र (aiṁ klīṁ sauḥ) and its greatness.
Paṭala 3 (36 verses)
In the beginning अन्तर्याग or inner worship is described as meditation on the deity mūlavidyā in the मूलाधार-चक्र.
This is followed by a detailed description of बहिर्याग or external worship including the drawing of a यन्त्र.
At the end is given a long description of the goddess Tripureśvarī and meditation on her.
Paṭala 4 (81 verses)
This paṭala gives an account of the method of worship of the goddess Tripureśvarī, including various complicated mudrās or poses of fingers.
Towards the end is described the worship of ten Bhairavas like Hetuka and Tripurāntaka as also of others like the eight वसुस् and eleven Rudras.
Paṭala 5 (49 verses)
Worship of Tripureśvarī with various items along with the appropriate mudrās is continued here.
Paṭala 6 (35 verses)
Worship of the same deity as seated on the pūrvasiṁhāsana (the throne in the east) is described here.
Paṭala 7 (21 verses)
This paṭala narrates the पूजा (worship), the ध्यान (meditation) and the यन्त्र (mystical diagram) of त्रिपुर-भैरवी.
Paṭala 8 (16 verses)
The goddess Bhariravī is sitting on the paścimasiṁhāsana (the throne in the west). meditation on her as also her यन्त्र are narrated here.
Paṭala 9 (86 verses)
In this section, the mantras of भुवनेश्वरी-भैरवी, अन्नपूर्णा, Varāhā and Kubjikā are given.
Paṭala 10 (103 verses)
The method of drawing the श्रीचक्र and the ṣaḍadhvās—the six paths that lead to the देवी like Varṇādhvā and tattvādhvā—are described here.
Paṭala 11 (11 verses)
Kāmeśvarī-मन्त्र of five letters is given here.
Paṭala 12 (26 verses)
The पञ्चदशाक्षरी-मन्त्र (mantra of 15 letters) given by लोपामुद्रा (Agastya’s wife), known as the ‘Hādividyā’, is described here. Other mantras attri-buted to मनु, चन्द्र (Moon), कुबेर, अगस्त्य, नन्द, इन्द्र, सूर्य, शङ्कर, Nandikeśvara and दुर्वासस् are also mentioned.
Paṭala 13 (52 verses)
This deals with the ṣoḍaśākṣarī-विद्या or मन्त्र (of the देवी) with 16 letters, its eulogy and the warning that it should be ceremonially received from a competent गुरु.
Paṭala 14 (148 verses)
The topics dealt with in this section are: worship of the श्रीविद्या, establishing the कलश (pot of holy water); the मन्त्र of Ānandabhairava; various nyāsas like sarvasaubhāgyasundarīnyāsa, sammohana- न्यास, Gaṇeśamātṛkānyāsa and so on.
Paṭala 15 (69 verses)
The following are the subjects dealt with here: the 46 lettered मन्त्र of Kāmeśvarīnityā; other mantras like those of Bhagamālinī (145 letters), नित्य-klinnā (11 letters), Bheruṇḍa (10 letters), Vahnivāsinī (9 letters), Mahāvidyeśvarī (14 letters), शिवदूती (7 letters), Tvaritā (12 letters), Kulasundarī (3 letters), Nityā (14 letters), Nīlapatākinī (15 letters), Vijayā (7 letters), सर्वमङ्गला (9 letters), Jvālāmālinī (43 letters) and Vicitrā (1 letter).
Then some special mudrās like saṅkṣobha, ākarṣaṇa and khecarī are described.
Paṭala 16 (228 verses)
This is the longest paṭala. The contents may briefly be given as follows: अन्तर्याग (internal meditation on the देवी); worship of the गुरु; worship of the gods in the four cardinal directions through the श्रीचक्र; worship of the five ‘pañcikās’ (groups of five deities) like Kośapañcikā and Kāmadhenupañcikā, each comprising five goddesses; several mantras like those of महालक्ष्मी, Pārijāteśī and Mahāvidyā (total seven mantras); worship of the various चक्रस् of the श्रीचक्र; closing of the pūjās.
Paṭala 17 (118 verses)
This paṭala deals with the following subjects: various kinds of japamālās (rosaries) made of pearls, रुद्राक्ष beads (Elaeocarpus ganitrus), māṇikya (ruby) and padmākṣa (lotus seeds) as also their special results; पुरश्चरण of the mantras (See PURAŚCARAṆA under TANTRAS); using the श्रीविद्या to fulfil one’s desires; different desires fulfilled by worshipping the goddess by different flowers.
Paṭala 18 (26 verses)
By worshipping the देवी with golden flowers in which precious stones such as diamond, sapphire, topaz, coral, ruby, pearl, opal etc., are set, for the prescribed numbers of days, the aspirant can reap many miraculous results such as controlling human beings, gods and animals etc. This is the gist of this chapter.
Paṭala 19 (44 verses)
Three aspects of the goddess, viz., Tripurāmbā, Vāgīśvarī and कामकला are described here along with their modes of worship, ध्यान (meditation) and the results obtained.
Paṭala 20 (179 verses)
The जप and होम connected with the worship of Tripurādevī are described here in detail.
The following is a brief synopsis of the contents: Three kinds of जप of the मन्त्र (nigada, upāṁśu and mānasa); preparing the homakuṇḍa (pit for performing होम); arranging the dīpa (lamp and समिध् (fuel faggots); worship of the fire-god; general होम and special होम for the fulfilment of desires; instructions regarding dik (direction), नक्षत्र (stars or asterism), vāra (weekday), samaya (time), carma (skin-seats) and samit (fuel faggots) suitable for different results while undertaking the षट्कर्मस् (See ṢAṬKARMAS.); पूर्णाहुति (final offering).
Paṭala 21 (34 verses)
Jñānayajña is described here. The sādhaka has to offer mentally all the letters of the alphabet, his पुण्य and पाप (religious merit and demerit), good and bad deeds, धर्म and अधर्म into his own आत्मन्. This leads to the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्.
Paṭala 22 (74 verses)
This chapter describes Kumārīpūjā (worship of a girl before puberty, as the goddess) as also some वामाचार rites.
Paṭala 23 (36 verses)
Four kinds of आत्मन् (for inner contemplation viz., Ātmā, Antarātmā, Paramātmā and Jñānātmā) and four types of dūtīs (women-helpers) are described here.
Paṭala 24 (96 verses)
This section deals with the method of दीक्षा or initiation. The topics described are: preparation of a मण्डप or shed; establishment of kalaśas, or water pots ceremonially filled up; persons unfit for दीक्षा; persons fit for receiving दीक्षा; actual method of दीक्षा involving the famous Vedāntic dictum tat-tvam-asi; about the seven चक्रस् like मूलाधार and स्वाधिष्ठान; giving the Ṣoḍaśākṣarī mantra; greatness of this मन्त्र; days of एच्लिप्से of the sun and the मोओन् are extremely auspicious to give or receive दीक्षा; certain months like चैत्र (March/April) and आषाढ (July) are considered inauspicious for दीक्षा.
Paṭala 25 (23 verses)
Preparation of the पवित्र (a ring made of कुश grass Poa cynosuroides) purified by offering it to the goddess and wearing it—are described here.
Paṭala 26 (31 verses)
This last section describes the worship of Damanaka (a kind of plant or creeper) as also of मन्मथ along with his two consorts, रति and Prīti.

jñāna
(‘knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
Derived from the root-verb ‘jñā’ (= to know) the word ‘jñāna’ is commonly interpreted as ‘knowledge’.
This knowledge is of two kinds: that which is got by the normal means of sense perception and that which is obtained by intuition.
Most of the philosophical systems accept three sources of knowledge: प्रत्यक्ष (direct perception), अनुमान (inference) and āptavākya (verbal testimony) or āgama (scriptural testimony).
Sometimes three more are added, taking the total to six. Those are: उपमान (comparison), अर्थापत्ति (postulation) and अनुपलब्धि (non-perception).
Jñāna as intuitive knowledge—called ‘aparokṣānubhūti’ (direct experience)—comes through the purification of the मिन्द् by yogic disciplines and meditation on आत्मन्/Brahman or God.

Jñāneśvar, Sant
(A.

-1296)
------------------------------------------
If हिन्दुइस्म् has survived in spite of external aggressions, and internal upheavals, it is not a little due to the galaxy of the teachers of the भक्ति Movement, over several centuries.
Sant JñāneśvarSant Jñāneśvar (also known as Jñānadev) is the brightest jewel among the saints of Maharashtra. He was born as the second son of Viṭṭhala Pant and Rakhumā Bāī in A.

at आऌअन्दी near Pune in Maharashtra. निवृत्ति was his elder brother. Sopāna and मुक्ताबाई were his younger brother and sister.
Viṭṭhala Pant had taken सṁन्यास from the well-known saint रामानन्द of Kāśi by telling him a lie that he had no dependents. Actually, he had been married to Rakhumābāī who had not permitted him for सṁन्यास, which was necessary. When रामानन्द came to know of this, he was furious and sent Viṭṭhala Pant back to his wife.
Since he had returned to the life of a householder after सṁन्यास, which was considered as a heinous sin, the contemporary society had boycotted him. Hence, the children born, could not be administered the sacraments normal to the Hindu ब्राह्मणस्. So, he and his wife drowned themselves in a river, leaving the children as orphans.
However, the children, by the dint of their learning and yogic powers, earned the respect of the society.
Nivṛtti, the eldest of them, was a highly evolved सोउल्. He was blessed with spiritual wisdom by a great saint Gayanī-nāth. निवृत्ति in turn initiated Jñāneśvar also into the mysteries of spiritual wisdom.
Many miracles have been attributed to Jñāneśvar. Some of them are: making a bison repeat the Vedic mantras; bringing a dead person back to life; travelling in the air sitting upon an old brick wall, to meet a haṭhayogi called चाङ्गदेव, who was coming on a tiger and so on.
The greatest work of Jñāneśvar was composing the immortal treatise Bhāvārthadīpikā—more popularly known as the Jñāneśvarī—a detailed commentary in Marāṭhī, on the Bhagavadgītā. Actually, it was a series of his discourses on the Gītā delivered in a temple in a village called Neveśe.
He has also composed a few अभङ्गस् or devotional songs.
He left his body in a state of deep समाधि in A.

at the young age of 21, at आऌअन्दी. His समाधि has now become a famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे.
His teachings are a balanced combination of ज्ञान (knowledge) and भक्ति (devotion to God).
Many saints of Maharashtra like नाम्देव्, Sāvatā Mālī, Narahari Sonār, Janābāī, Gorākuṁhār and Cokhamelā were his contemporaries.

jñānaśakti
(‘power of knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
Hiraṇyagarbha (= of golden womb) is the second aspect of ब्रह्मन् after ईश्वर. He has three powers of which ज्ञानशक्ति (= power of knowledge) is also one. By this power he knows everything.
See also HIRAṆYAGARBHA, ĪCCHĀŚAKTI and KRIYĀŚAKTI.

Jñānakāṇḍa
(‘branch [of the Veda devoted to] spiritual wisdom’)
------------------------------------------
The वेदस् are the foundational scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्. According to one of the methods of dividing them, they comprise three parts: कर्मकाण्ड, Upāsanā-kāṇḍa and ज्ञानकाण्ड.
The Saṁhitā and the ब्राह्मण parts of the वेदस् deal mainly with कर्म or Vedic rituals. Hence they are classified under the heading ‘Karmakāṇḍa’.
The उपनिषद्स्, which often form a part of the Āraṇyaka section, deal with ज्ञान (spiritual knowledge or wisdom) and hence are called ‘Jñānakāṇḍa’.
The portions of the आरण्यकस्, including some of the उपनिषद्स्, which teach upāsanās or special kinds of meditations (also called ‘vidyās’), are grouped under the title, ‘Upāsanākāṇḍa’.
However, the last classification is, comparatively speaking, less common.

Jñānayoga
------------------------------------------
Human beings are essentially divine. The divinity within—called ‘ātman’—has to be rediscovered, fully manifested and experienced. Once this is achieved, the cycle of transmigration ceases for ever. This is the goal of life and is variously termed as मुक्ति or मोक्ष, कैवल्य and निर्वाण.
Traditional हिन्दुइस्म्, as reflected in the Vedāntic scriptures and their commentaries, generally accepts two paths of sādhanās or spiritual disciplines, to this मोक्ष. They are ज्ञान (knowledge) and भक्ति (devotion). (See BHAKTI and BHAKTIYOGA.)
Abandonment of selfish and desire-motivated actions and sincere performance of ordained duties leads to cittaśuddhi or purification of मिन्द्. Practice of the aṣṭāṅgayoga (the योग prescribed by पतञ्जलि, consisting of eight graded steps) helps in developing concentration of मिन्द्. Both these spiritual disciplines have been accepted as aids to the practice of ज्ञान and भक्ति.
The basic texts of Vedānta, viz., the प्रस्थानत्रय (the उपनिषद्स्, the Brahmasūtras and the Bhagavadgītā) have described two types of मुक्ति: the sadyomukti (instant लिबेरतिओन्) and the क्रममुक्ति (gradual लिबेरतिओन्). Two more terms which are the approximate equivalents of these are: जीवन्मुक्ति (liberation even while living in this body) and videhamukti (liberation after the fall of the body).
Performance of one’s ordained duties coupled with contemplation on the Vedic deities results in क्रममुक्ति (gradual लिबेरतिओन्) of the जीव (the individual सोउल्) by taking to the Arcīrādimārga (the path of light) and going to ब्रह्मलोक (the world of ब्रह्मा, the creator). Final लिबेरतिओन् will come on the dissolution of the ब्रह्मलोक at the end of the cycle of च्रेअतिओन्.
Sadyomukti (instant लिबेरतिओन्) however, comes from ज्ञान resulting from ज्ञानयोग. Though the word ‘jñāna’ derived from the verbal root jñā means knowledge, it has a higher philosophical connotation in Vedāntic works. It is not only intellectual knowledge but also intuitive experience. It starts with the former and ends with the latter.
But this has to be accomplished gradually.
Firstly, a person has to attain चित्त-शुद्धि or a fair degree of purity of मिन्द् by discharging his duties and responsibilities as prescribed by the holy books.
Secondly, he has to cultivate sādhana-catuṣṭaya or the fourfold Vedāntic discipline.
Thirdly, he has to approach a compe-tent गुरु, learn the truths of Vedānta from him and contemplate on them, which will ultimately result in the direct experience of the आत्मन्.
These three may now be described more fully.
Cittaśuddhi or purity of मिन्द् is attained by avoiding all actions and types of behaviour opposed to the principles of धर्म or righteousness; by giving up all actions motivated by selfish desires and, by performing the ordained duties to the best of one’s ability as service to mankind as also to please God.
The साधनचतुष्टय comprises the following disciplines:
Viveka or discrimination between the real (the आत्मन्, the सोउल्) and the unreal (the evanescent world);
Vairāgya or the spirit of renunciation resulting in giving up the evanescent things of the world, for the sake of realising the आत्मन्;
Śamādiṣaṭka or cultivation of the six qualities viz., शम (peace of मिन्द्), दम (control of senses), उपरति (withdrawal of senses and not allowing them to go towards the sense-objects once again), तितिक्षा (forbearance), श्रद्धा (faith in the scriptures, in the teachers and in oneself) and समाधान (concentration of मिन्द्);
Mumukṣutva or intense desire for मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
Once a person is fired by the intense desire for मोक्ष, he will approach a गुरु or a competent spiritual teacher—this is called ‘gurūpasadana’—in search of ज्ञान or knowledge that can give him मोक्ष.
The गुरु should be not only well-versed in the scriptural lore, knowing their true essence, but also be a person of spiritual attainment.
Once he is convinced about the fitness of the aspiring disciple, he will teach him the Vedāntic truths as described in the प्रस्थानत्रय and also from his own experience. The disciple should do śravaṇa or hear it attentively. After clearing his doubts through questioning and मनन or reflection, he should do निदिध्यासन or meditation on the truth as comprehended by him, viz., that the nature of his own आत्मन् or the Self is pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, completely separate and different from the body-मिन्द् complex. This meditation will ultimately result in the aparokṣānubhava or the direct experience of one’s true nature as the आत्मन्. Once this experience is gained, he will become mukta or liberated. He may continue to live in the body for some more time due to the effect of the प्रारब्धकर्म which has started the present birth. In this state he is known as a jīvanmukta (one who is liberated even while living). Non-attachment and universal love are his chief characteristics.
At the end of this life, when प्रारब्धकर्म gets exhausted, he becomes a videhamukta, totally liberated from all future bodies too.

Jñānasambandhar
------------------------------------------
Nāyanmārs or नायनार्स् are the great Śaiva saints of Tamil Nadu who revived शैविस्म् when जैनिस्म् was having its heydays. Though 63 of them have been listed, only four of them have been very famous. Perhaps, the most well-known even among them was ज्ञानसम्बन्धर्, also known as Tirujñānasambandhar or just सम्बन्धर्.
It is said that when his parents—Śivapādahṛdayar and Bhagavatiyār—had left him, as a baby, on the bank of a Kalyāṇī (temple-tank) while taking their bath, he started crying and was breast-fed by the Divine मोथेर् पार्वती herself. Since then he developed the power of composing devotional poems of exquisite literary grace, on Lord शिव.
He travelled extensively all over the land of Tamil Nadu, often with other well-known saints like Nīlakaṇṭhayāḷ Pānār (an accomplished player of the Vīṇā or lute) and अप्पर् (a senior contemporary and himself a great saint).
He is credited to have performed many miracles, at the request of the distressed people. Some of them are: curing the daughter of the king Māḷava, of her serious incurable disease; dispelling the severe cold wave which had hit the village Śaṅgunrūr; getting gold coins through divine intervention for his ड़थेर् who wanted to perform a great sacrifice; reviving a dead merchant at a place called Tirumarugāḷ; converting the king of मदुरै to शैविस्म् by exhibiting divine miracles and also curing him of a fell disease; converting many Jains and Buddhists back to शैविस्म्; reviving Pūmpāvai, the daughter of Śivaneśar to life, from her ashes and so on.
He was married to the daughter of Nambāṇḍar Nambi. The wonder of wonders was that immediately after the मर्रिअगे, the couple as also all the others who had gathered there were absorbed into the divine light that emerged from Lord शिव who appeared before them.
Jñānasambandhar was also known as Piḷḷai Nāyanār (child devotee of शिव). He perhaps lived in the 7th-8th century A. D. His songs, as available today, number 4168. They are all musical compositions set to various tunes of मुसिच्.
